If you adopted some manner of voting besides plurality ("winner take all"), you could minimize the impact of the two major parties. Condorcet, Instant Run Off, or others could be used. This certainly doesn't get rid of political parties, however: it actually increases their number. It does force them to work together more, and removes a lot of the power currently held by the unelected portions of the Republicans and Democrats.

To get rid of political parties in general would require a serious change, and therefore a risky one. Political parties are emergent- that is, given the rules of democracy, they happen automatically because democracies select for them. They select for them because the entire point of the democracy is that the politicians work together to make laws. If there are, say, 100 lawmakers who all vote their heart (or the views of their constituents), then this works as Jefferson and others intended. But if politician Alfred talks to politicians Bob and Charles, and proposes that, on the upcoming two votes, Alfred votes in a way that Bob and Charles like (that he would otherwise not have done) on the first one, while Bob and Charles both vote in a way that Alfred would like on the second one, then Alfred, Bob, and Charles are in some ways a political party. The first issue was very important to Bob and Charles, and the second issue very important to Alfred.

As long as politicians have names, make deals, and exist in public, there will always be serious rewards for teaming up like this. Further, Dennis now has a motivation to join up with Alfred, Bob, and Charles, or find a group of his own that will help him- he may have been deeply disappointed to see Bob and Charles voting the way they did on the first issue, or he may have been opposed to both votes.

It's now in everyone's interest to team up, because they can't deliver any vote but their own. Throw in the fact that you can much more easily get concessions for your region or people from team ABC if you routinely talk with them, and it's clear that political parties will emerge regardless. The plurality voting system ensures that there will always be exactly two, with very small blips in between.

Anyway, the answer to your question would be either a direct democracy, or a more complex system that puts several types of issue to direct vote, while allowing representatives to handle others. Even that second one is only theoretical, because you only need to distract the voters briefly to take away their direct democracy. Plus, of course, direct democracy has many other issues.

One common sciency explanation for the existence of the universe is a multiversal one where a black hole results in the birth of a daughter universe. But like the title says, this implies the mother universe was born in a black hole as well, which implies another universe also born in a black hole; we're no better off than we are when the question is "Where did God come from?". But we already have precedent for matter being finite and, when it turned out that wasn't true, it was because energy was finite; in both cases, something can only be shifted from one form to another.

But what if, like the law of conservation of matter, the law of conservation of energy is wrong in favor of a more general law of conservation of universes? In the event of a universe reaching maximum entropy(like a Big Crunch or a Big Rip), the laws of physics break down and the universe undergoes a "phase shift" into one with a new set of laws that mean it's now at *minimum* entropy - so what we currently see as the "birth" of our universe was merely it taking on a new form. This pretty much invalidates the entire question, doesn't it?
To avoid the turtle problem, universes have to be conserved like matter was thought to be and energy is currently believed to be.
